cards.front: What makes a web tier **stateless**, and why does it matter for scaling?
cards.back: No user data (sessions, carts, uploads) is kept on the instance itself. Any instance can then answer any request, so an Auto Scaling group can add, remove or replace instances freely.

cards.front: Why is an Elastic IP not a way to scale a web fleet?
cards.back: One Elastic IP maps to one instance, and accounts get **5 per Region** by default. It gives a fixed address (and can be remapped after a failure), but no load spreading. Every public IPv4 address, Elastic IPs included, is billed hourly.
cards.updated: Public IPv4 addresses, including attached Elastic IPs, have been billed at USD 0.005 per hour since February 2024.

cards.front: What goes wrong when you scale out by listing every instance IP in a DNS A record with a 1-hour TTL?
cards.back: Clients cache the answer for up to an hour, so when an instance is terminated they keep calling a dead IP and get errors; you also have to edit the record whenever the fleet changes.

cards.front: Which Route 53 record type should point a domain at a load balancer, and what is special about its TTL?
cards.back: An **alias** record (type A or AAAA). You cannot set its TTL; Route 53 follows the load balancer's changing IPs itself. It works at the zone apex and alias queries to AWS resources are free.

cards.front: In the WhatIsTheTime.com design, what does the load balancer add, and what does the Auto Scaling group add?
cards.back: **ELB**: one endpoint, health checks that skip broken instances, private instances behind it. **Auto Scaling group**: launches, registers and replaces instances automatically and follows the load.

cards.front: Which part of a web fleet is worth covering with Reserved Instances or Savings Plans?
cards.back: The **minimum capacity** that runs 24/7 (for example min 2 instances across two AZs). Capacity above the baseline stays On-Demand, or Spot if the app tolerates interruptions.
cards.updated: Today compare RIs with Savings Plans: EC2 Instance Savings Plans up to 72% off, Compute Savings Plans up to 66% off and flexible across families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda.

cards.front: How do sticky sessions keep a shopping cart, and what are their two weaknesses?
cards.back: The ALB sets a cookie (`AWSALB` or an application cookie) and keeps sending the client to the same instance. Weaknesses: load can become uneven, and the session is lost if that instance fails or is scaled in.

cards.front: What are the downsides of storing the whole shopping cart in a browser cookie?
cards.back: Every request gets heavier, users can tamper with the cookie (so it must be validated), and browsers only guarantee about **4 KB** per cookie.

cards.front: What is a server-side session store, and which AWS services fit it?
cards.back: The browser keeps only a `session_id` cookie; the session data lives in a shared store keyed by that ID. Use **ElastiCache** (Valkey, Redis OSS, Memcached) or **DynamoDB**, whose TTL can expire old sessions for free.

cards.front: Two ways to take read load off an RDS primary in the MyClothes.com design?
cards.back: **Read replicas** (asynchronous copies, up to 15 for MySQL, MariaDB and PostgreSQL; the app sends reads to them) or a **cache** such as ElastiCache with lazy loading in front of RDS.

cards.front: Describe **lazy loading** and its main drawbacks.
cards.back: Read the cache first; on a miss, query the database and write the result into the cache (ideally with a TTL). Drawbacks: a slow first request (three round trips) and possibly stale data until the TTL expires.

cards.front: Does a classic RDS Multi-AZ standby help with read scaling?
cards.back: No. The Multi-AZ DB instance standby is synchronous and only takes over on failure; it serves no queries. (The newer Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment has two standbys that can serve reads.)
cards.updated: Multi-AZ DB cluster deployments (two readable standbys in three AZs) are newer than the slides.

cards.front: Write the security group chain for a three-tier web app (ALB, app instances, RDS).
cards.back: ALB SG: 80/443 from `0.0.0.0/0`. App SG: app port from the **ALB SG**. RDS SG: 3306 (or engine port) from the **app SG**. Same pattern for ElastiCache.

cards.front: Why did MyWordPress.com move from RDS MySQL to Aurora MySQL?
cards.back: Aurora gives easy high availability and read scaling: storage replicated across three AZs, up to 15 Aurora Replicas on the shared volume with a reader endpoint, and automatic promotion of a replica if the writer fails.

cards.front: Why do uploaded images go missing when a multi-AZ WordPress fleet stores them on EBS?
cards.back: Each instance writes to its own EBS volume, which lives in one AZ and attaches to one instance. A reader routed to another instance has a different disk without the file.

cards.front: How does EFS let instances in several AZs share the same files?
cards.back: You create a **mount target** (an ENI with a private IP) in each AZ; instances mount the file system over NFS (port 2049) through the mount target in their AZ. A Regional file system stores data redundantly across AZs.

cards.front: What are the limits of EBS Multi-Attach?
cards.back: Only Provisioned IOPS `io1`/`io2` volumes, only instances in the **same AZ**, up to **16** Nitro-based instances, and you need a cluster-aware file system. Not a substitute for EFS.

cards.front: Golden AMI versus user data: what does each speed up?
cards.back: **Golden AMI**: OS packages, runtime and app pre-installed, so boot-to-ready is fast. **User data**: per-launch dynamic configuration (runs as root, first boot only by default, 16 KB limit). Combining both is the hybrid approach Elastic Beanstalk uses.

cards.front: What happens when you restore an RDS DB snapshot?
cards.back: RDS creates a **new** DB instance (new endpoint) with schemas and data already present; you cannot restore into an existing instance. Data loads lazily in the background, so first queries can be slower.

cards.front: How can you avoid slow first reads on an EBS volume restored from a snapshot?
cards.back: Use **fast snapshot restore**, set a **Provisioned Rate for Volume Initialization** (100 to 300 MiB/s, extra fee), or read every block once with `fio` or `dd`.
cards.updated: The provisioned volume initialization rate is newer than the slides.

cards.front: What does AWS Elastic Beanstalk cost, and what does it manage?
cards.back: No extra charge: you pay only for the EC2, ELB, RDS and other resources it creates. It handles provisioning, load balancing, scaling, health monitoring and platform updates; you bring the code and keep control of settings.

cards.front: Define Beanstalk **application**, **application version** and **environment**.
cards.back: **Application**: container for versions, environments and saved configurations. **Version**: one labelled build of your code stored in S3. **Environment**: the AWS resources running exactly one version at a time (for example dev and prod).

cards.front: How does a Beanstalk **worker environment** receive work?
cards.back: It has no load balancer. A daemon on each instance pulls messages from an **SQS queue** and HTTP POSTs them to the app on localhost; `200 OK` deletes the message, failures retry and end in a dead-letter queue. `cron.yaml` adds periodic tasks.

cards.front: Beanstalk single-instance versus load-balanced environment?
cards.back: **Single instance**: one EC2 with an Elastic IP, Auto Scaling group fixed at 1, for dev and test. **Load balanced**: ALB plus an Auto Scaling group across AZs (and optionally Multi-AZ RDS), for production.

cards.front: Which Beanstalk platforms from the slides no longer exist?
cards.back: Packer Builder (custom platforms), multi-container Docker (now the **ECS** platform) and Preconfigured Docker were retired with Amazon Linux AMI in July 2022. Current Linux platforms all run on Amazon Linux 2023.
cards.updated: AL1 branches retired 18 July 2022; the last Amazon Linux 2 branches retired 6 August 2026.

cards.front: Which Beanstalk deployment options avoid downtime and allow a fast rollback?
cards.back: **Immutable** (new instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group), **traffic splitting** (canary share of traffic, needs an ALB) and **blue/green** with **Swap environment URLs**. All at once (the default) causes brief downtime.

cards.front: Why should a production Beanstalk app not rely on a database coupled to its environment?
cards.back: A coupled RDS instance follows the environment's lifecycle (deletion policy Delete, Snapshot or Retain on termination) and is not carried across a blue/green swap. Keep production data in a decoupled or separately created database.

cards.front: What is Elastic Beanstalk Cluster mode?
cards.back: Launched 17 September 2026: environments run as container replicas on a Beanstalk-operated **EKS** cluster (EKS Auto Mode nodes) shared by environments on the same subnets. The EC2-based model is now called Beanstalk Standard.
cards.updated: New feature announced 17 September 2026, after the slides.

cards.front: Which Elastic Beanstalk environment settings are fixed once the environment is created?
cards.back: The **environment tier** (web server or worker) and the **load balancer type** (ALB, NLB or CLB). The environment type, single instance or load balanced, can still be switched later.

cards.front: In the typical three-tier web architecture, what goes in the public, private and data subnets?
cards.back: **Public**: the load balancer, which Route 53 targets with an alias record. **Private**: the Auto Scaling group of app instances, with no public IPs. **Data**: RDS and ElastiCache, reachable only from the app tier's security group.
